title: Open first browser content automatically and badge background activity
body:
## What

Make the session Browser’s attention behavior reflect actual browser content and activity:

- Automatically open Browser when the session receives its first real content.
- Respect the user’s tab choice after that first reveal.
- Show the Browser glow when new preview or agent-browser activity occurs while Browser is hidden.
- Clear the glow when Browser becomes visible.
- Reset the lifecycle after the preview is cleared, allowing the next first content to auto-open again.
- Clear stale navigation state when switching sessions.

Users can now continue working in Summary, Reviews, or Files without Browser repeatedly stealing focus, while still receiving a meaningful indicator when background browser work occurs.

## Why

The previous glow was driven by terminal-output URL detection rather than browser state.

Any HTTP(S) URL printed in the terminal—including replayed terminal history—could activate the Browser glow even when the Browser had no page to display. At the same time, a legitimate first preview did not automatically reveal Browser.

This made the indicator misleading: it could appear with nothing to show and did not reliably guide users to actual preview content.

## How

Browser attention is now driven by authoritative session state:

- A non-empty `previewUrl` or browser navigation URL begins a content lifecycle.
- The first content in that lifecycle selects Browser and expands the inspector.
- Later `ao preview` revisions glow when the user is viewing another inspector tab.
- Agent-browser commands also glow while Browser is hidden, including commands that do not navigate.
- Opening Browser consumes the unseen state.
- Clearing all browser content resets both the reveal and unseen state.
- Explicitly clicking a terminal link still opens Browser immediately and persists the selected target.

### Removed

- Removed `detect-urls.ts` and its tests.
- Removed terminal output decoding through `useTerminalSession.onOutput`.
- Removed the `TerminalPane` watcher that treated printed URLs as Browser activity.

These paths existed only to power the passive URL glow. Clickable terminal links use the separate xterm link handler and remain supported.

## Testing

- `npm test -- src/renderer/components/SessionView.test.tsx src/renderer/components/SessionInspector.test.tsx src/renderer/components/TerminalPane.test.tsx src/renderer/hooks/useBrowserView.test.tsx src/renderer/hooks/useTerminalSession.test.tsx`
  - 5 test files passed
  - 158 tests passed
- `npm run typecheck`
  - Passed
- Manually verified the Browser auto-open, background glow, glow clearing, and tab-preservation behavior in the desktop app.

## Checklist

- [x] Branched from `main`
- [x] One focused change
- [x] Follows `AGENTS.md` conventions and PR hygiene
- [x] Tests added or updated for the user-visible behavior
- [x] Relevant local frontend checks pass

title: Add immutable Chat/TUI session modes and structured orchestrator Chat
body:
## Problem

AO currently has one interaction model for a running agent session: launch the provider's native CLI/TUI inside the selected terminal runtime, then deliver later messages by pasting text and Enter into that pane.

That model is valuable for broad agent compatibility, native provider workflows, and terminal escape hatches, but it is not a reliable substrate for a first-class chat product:

- a successful pane write is not an agent delivery acknowledgement;
- terminal bytes do not provide durable, typed conversation history;
- tool calls, diffs, plans, permissions, streaming deltas, usage, and errors must be inferred from terminal output or separate hooks;
- a keystroke intended as a prompt can land in a permission dialog or shell;
- a Chat UI backed by an SDK while a native TUI remains writable would create two independent conversation controllers that can diverge.

The unsafe design is:

```text
Chat UI -> Claude SDK / Codex app-server -> provider conversation A
Terminal -> native Claude/Codex TUI      -> provider conversation B (or a racing client on A)
```

Even if both clients start with the same provider conversation ID, concurrent writers can race on turns, permissions, compaction, model/mode changes, and reconnect state.

AO should instead let the user choose a **default session interface**:

- **Chat**: AO starts and owns a structured provider controller (Claude Agent SDK, Codex app-server, ACP, or another supported machine protocol). Chat is the default session surface. The Terminal option opens a plain shell in the same worktree, not a second native agent TUI.
- **Terminal UI (TUI)**: AO behaves as it does today. The provider's native TUI is the only conversation controller and the session opens in the existing terminal experience.

This must be a durable, immutable per-session controller mode, not merely a preferred tab. The global preference selects the mode for newly created sessions; every later spawn, send, restore, activity, permission, and UI decision uses the mode stored on the session.

## User outcome

As an AO user, I can choose **Chat** or **Terminal UI** as my default session interface.

When I choose Chat:

- newly created orchestrators open in a first-class Chat UI;
- workers spawned later use Chat when their selected harness has a production-ready structured driver;
- desktop, mobile, `ao send`, browser annotations, orchestrator coordination, and automated reactions all feed the same AO-owned conversation controller;
- I can open a normal shell in the session worktree without starting a second copy of the agent;
- messages, streaming output, tool calls, permissions, diffs, plans/todos, errors, and usage are represented as structured events;
- daemon/app restarts resume the same provider conversation.

When I choose Terminal UI:

- newly created sessions use the current native TUI workflow;
- the session opens in the current terminal view;
- existing terminal delivery, hooks, restore, and runtime behavior remain intact;
- no structured SDK/app-server controller is started for that session.

Changing the preference affects **future sessions only**. It never changes the controller of an existing session.

## Final architecture

```text
Daemon setting
defaultSessionMode = chat | tui
             ↓
Spawn resolves and persists immutable session.mode
             ↓
      ┌──────┴──────┐
      │             │
 mode=chat       mode=tui
      │             │
Conversation     Native Agent
Controller       + tmux/conpty
      │             │
Codex app-server Existing guarded pane delivery
over stdio
      │
Provider thread
```

For the project orchestrator, the durable human-facing conversation is project-scoped even though the runtime session is replaceable:

```text
Project conversation
├── ordered turns and items
├── durable actions
├── delegation records
└── current orchestrator binding
        ├── AO session ID
        ├── provider conversation ID
        └── controller generation
```

Worker conversations remain session-scoped.

The first production Chat provider is **Codex app-server over its default stdio transport**. Claude Agent SDK is the second structured provider after the provider-neutral contract and Codex vertical slice are proven. Chat mode does not use Codex remote TUI attachment, WebSocket transport, or a provider TUI as an approval fallback.

## Required invariants

These are load-bearing acceptance rules, not implementation suggestions:

1. **Exactly one controller per session.** A live session has one effective mode and one active conversation controller.
2. **Mode is immutable.** `session.mode` is chosen before controller launch, persisted with the session, and cannot be patched later.
3. **Settings affect only new sessions.** Changing `defaultSessionMode` never mutates existing rows or restarts existing controllers.
4. **Server-side enforcement.** The daemon dispatches from the persisted session mode. UI visibility alone is not a safety boundary.
5. **All senders share one dispatcher.** Desktop, mobile, CLI, browser annotations, lifecycle reactions, reviewer results, orchestrator notices, and internal coordination cannot bypass mode-aware routing.
6. **Chat mode never launches the native agent TUI.** Its Terminal action creates/opens only a session-scoped shell terminal.
7. **TUI mode never launches a structured chat driver.** It continues to use the existing runtime/pane path.
8. **No silent fallback.** If Chat is requested for an unsupported or unhealthy harness, creation fails with a typed error and the client may offer an explicit “Create as TUI” action.
9. **Explicit fallback is decided before creation.** Choosing “Create as TUI” produces a TUI session from birth; it does not start Chat and then switch.
10. **Existing sessions remain TUI.** The migration backfills every pre-feature session to `tui`.
11. **Wrong-generation events are ignored.** Events from a dead/replaced Chat controller cannot mutate the current session.
12. **Provider context has one owner.** AO controls provider input ordering; clients never invoke provider transports directly.
13. **PTY output is not chat history.** No code converts raw terminal bytes into canonical assistant/tool messages.
14. **Structured events are authoritative in Chat mode.** Existing native hooks/terminal markers remain authoritative in TUI mode and must not race Chat projections.
15. **Terminal availability does not imply conversation availability.** A Chat shell can outlive or fail independently from the structured provider controller, and vice versa.
16. **Orchestrator conversation identity is project-scoped.** Replacing the orchestrator changes the runtime binding, not the human-facing conversation ID.
17. **Orchestrator replacement preserves mode by default.** A clean replacement inherits the current orchestrator's persisted mode unless an explicit creation-time mode change is requested.
18. **Native-context discontinuity is explicit.** If a replacement cannot resume the provider conversation, AO appends a system boundary and never pretends native context survived.

## Current architecture affected

The implementation should preserve current daemon/API boundaries and work from these existing seams:

| Area | Existing seam and required change |
|---|---|
| `backend/internal/domain/session.go` | `SessionRecord` lacks controller mode; `SessionMetadata` runtime IDs describe the native-TUI path and cannot identify a structured stream. |
| `backend/internal/ports/session.go` | Add requested/effective mode to `SpawnConfig`. |
| `backend/internal/ports/agent.go` | Keep the native CLI contract; do not stretch it into the structured conversation protocol. |
| `backend/internal/ports/outbound.go` | Replace direct use of terminal-specific `AgentMessenger` at shared send call sites with mode-aware dispatch. |
| `backend/internal/session_manager/manager.go` | Split `Manager.Spawn`/`Manager.Send` after persisted-mode resolution: native runtime for TUI, conversation controller for Chat. |
| `backend/internal/daemon/lifecycle_wiring.go` | Replace the unconditional `runtimeMessenger` boundary with the unified dispatcher. |
| `backend/internal/sessionguard/guard.go` | Retain pane-write safety for TUI; it is not the Chat send policy. |
| `backend/internal/terminal/doc.go` | Preserve raw PTY bytes as ephemeral transport, never canonical Chat events. |
| `backend/internal/storage/sqlite/migrations/0001_init.sql` and `queries/sessions.sql` | Add a new migration and update queries for durable mode/controller facts; preserve trigger-backed CDC. |
| `backend/internal/domain/projectconfig.go` | Add the daemon-owned default rather than a renderer-only preference. |
| `backend/internal/httpd/controllers/dto.go` and `sessions.go` | Add mode/capabilities/conversation DTOs and route `/sessions/{id}/send` through the dispatcher. |
| `backend/internal/service/session/service.go` | Make spawns, retire notices, and internal sends mode-aware. |
| `frontend/src/renderer/components/SessionView.tsx` and `CenterPane.tsx` | Select authoritative Chat or TUI surface from persisted mode; reuse session shell terminals for Chat. |
| `frontend/src/renderer/components/settings/GeneralSettingsSection.tsx` and `stores/ui-store.ts` | Read/write the daemon setting; local UI state is not authoritative. |
| `frontend/src/renderer/lib/spawn-orchestrator.ts` and `components/NewTaskDialog.tsx` | Carry requested mode and render typed unsupported-provider recovery. |
| `backend/internal/storage/sqlite/migrations/0027_shell_terminals.sql` and `0036_add_shell_terminal_session_id.sql` | Reuse the existing Chat-mode shell escape hatch. |

## Product behavior

### General setting

Add a daemon-backed setting:

```text
Default session interface
  Chat
  Terminal UI
```

Requirements:

- default to `tui` on upgrade for backward compatibility;
- explain that it applies to newly created sessions;
- expose a concise capability warning when Chat is selected;
- update through a daemon API so desktop, mobile, CLI, and headless spawns resolve one value;
- store under AO's existing `~/.ao` data boundary;
- do not use only Electron localStorage;
- do not mutate live sessions when changed.

Suggested copy:

> Controls how new orchestrator and worker sessions talk to their agent. Chat uses a supported structured agent connection. Terminal UI uses the agent's native terminal interface. Existing sessions are unchanged.

### Chat-mode session screen

The central session surface should be:

```text
Session
├── Chat (default and authoritative)
├── Terminal (plain worktree shell)
└── Inspector (summary, changes, PRs, files, browser, reviews)
```

Chat must support:

- initial prompt and follow-up user messages;
- streaming assistant content;
- stable message/turn identity;
- tool-call start/progress/completion;
- command, cwd, exit status, stdout/stderr, and duration where provided;
- file changes and diffs;
- plans/todos and progress state;
- permission/request-user-input cards with explicit decisions;
- interrupt/cancel;
- steering only when the driver declares it;
- queued follow-ups when steering is unavailable;
- structured errors and reconnect state;
- session resume/replay;
- token/cost/usage when provided;
- links, code blocks, copy actions, and accessible keyboard behavior;
- scroll anchoring that does not yank the user away from history;
- unread/new-output indication when the user is scrolled up;
- loading, empty, unsupported, crashed, reconnecting, and terminated states.

The Terminal action must use the existing session-scoped `shell_terminals` workflow. It must not attach to or launch the provider's native TUI.

### TUI-mode session screen

Keep the existing central terminal experience:

- native provider TUI remains the only conversation controller;
- existing shell/reviewer tabs continue to work;
- current send, terminal mux, hooks, activity, resume, and runtime safety remain intact;
- Chat is either hidden or replaced with a non-interactive explanation that this session was created in Terminal UI mode;
- no Chat driver process is started.

### Explicit one-off override

The first implementation may omit a per-spawn selector if the global setting is sufficient. The API/domain should nevertheless distinguish:

- no mode requested: resolve `defaultSessionMode`;
- explicit `chat` or `tui`: validate and persist that value.

This supports:

- “Create as TUI” after a typed unsupported-Chat failure;
- CLI/headless automation that needs deterministic behavior;
- future project/role defaults without changing session semantics.

An override is a creation-time input, never a live-session toggle.

### Unsupported Chat provider

Strict behavior is preferred:

```text
requested mode = chat
driver missing/unhealthy/incompatible
  -> reject before durable session/worktree creation where possible
  -> return typed capability error
  -> client offers explicit TUI creation
```

Do not silently create a TUI session. Silent fallback makes the setting untrustworthy and can put the user into a native terminal experience they deliberately disabled.

## Configuration resolution

Recommended precedence for a spawn:

1. explicit request mode, if present;
2. future project/role override, if introduced;
3. daemon-owned user `defaultSessionMode`;
4. compatibility default `tui`.

The effective mode must be resolved before the controller launches and written into the seed session record.

The harness and mode are separate decisions:

```text
harness = claude-code | codex | opencode | ...
mode    = chat | tui
```

A harness may implement:

- TUI only;
- Chat only in the future;
- both, selectable per session.

Do not encode modes as new harness names such as `claude-chat` or `codex-tui`; that would duplicate agent configuration and make capability discovery harder.

## Durable model and migration

Add a new SQLite migration; never edit an already-merged migration.

Minimum session facts:

```text
sessions.session_mode                  TEXT NOT NULL CHECK IN ('chat', 'tui')
sessions.provider_conversation_id      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''
sessions.controller_generation         TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''
```

Naming may change during implementation, but the concepts must remain explicit.

Migration rules:

- add `session_mode` with/backfilled to `tui`;
- existing `agent_session_id` compatibility must be audited before deciding whether to reuse, rename, or supersede it;
- do not conflate terminal `runtime_launch_id` with a Chat controller generation;
- include new fields in session insert/update/get/list queries;
- regenerate sqlc from query/migration sources;
- update storage round-trip and migration tests;
- update CDC session payloads only where clients need mode/controller state;
- use DB triggers for durable Chat event CDC rather than manual parallel store emission.

### Conversation persistence

Use a small stable durable core rather than a table or schema migration for every provider event subtype:

| Durable concept | Scope and purpose | Important identity |
|---|---|---|
| `conversations` | Project-scoped orchestrator narrative or session-scoped worker narrative | scope kind/id, current orchestrator binding, predecessor/boundary metadata |
| `conversation_turns` | One user/automation request and the agent work that follows | conversation, handling AO session, controller generation, provider turn ID, state |
| `conversation_items` | One ordered readable unit: message, activity, approval, delegation, summary, error, or system boundary | conversation sequence, revision, kind, origin, provider item ID |
| `conversation_commands` | Crash-safe provider-bound command/outbox row | conversation + client message ID, command state, provider request ID |
| `conversation_actions` | Crash-safe AO operation requested from Chat | idempotency key, request message, target, confirmation, state, typed result/error |
| `conversation_provider_state` | Provider binding, cursor, controller lease/generation, health | AO session + provider binding |
| `conversation_provider_events` | Dedupe for provider events that have stable native IDs | AO session + provider event ID |
| `session_delegations` | Orchestrator-to-worker assignment and action correlation | orchestrator session/turn, worker session, action, assignment |

Suggested stable core:

```text
Conversation
  id
  scope_kind: project | session
  project_id
  worker_session_id?
  current_orchestrator_session_id?
  predecessor_conversation_id?
  created_at
  updated_at

Turn
  id
  conversation_id
  handled_by_session_id
  provider_turn_id?
  controller_generation
  state
  requested_at
  started_at?
  completed_at?

Item
  id
  conversation_id
  turn_id?
  sequence
  revision
  kind
  role?
  origin
  sender_session_id?
  automation_kind?
  status
  text?
  summary?
  detail_json?

Command
  id
  conversation_id
  client_message_id
  command_kind
  state
  attempt_count
  provider_request_id?
  last_error?

Action
  id
  conversation_id
  requested_by_item_id
  action_type
  state
  target_session_id?
  target_pr_id?
  arguments_json
  confirmation_required
  idempotency_key
  request_id?
  error_code?
```

Initial item kinds:

```text
message
activity
approval
changed_files
delegation
coordination_summary
error
system
```

Provider-specific detail stays inside typed item projections. Unknown native events may be retained as bounded diagnostics, but they do not automatically become timeline semantics.

Ordering rules:

- conversation item `sequence` is immutable and conversation-scoped;
- item `revision` increases when streaming changes one existing item;
- timestamps are display metadata, not primary ordering;
- provider events from an inactive controller generation/lease are rejected;
- provider event IDs deduplicate observations;
- private/raw reasoning is never accepted into the normalized model;
- message origin is a durable field: `human`, `worker`, `orchestrator`, `automation`, `daemon`, or `provider`;
- worker/automation identity is stored structurally, never inferred from text prefixes.

### Project-scoped orchestrator continuity

The orchestrator runtime is replaceable; the project conversation is not.

On clean orchestrator replacement:

1. refetch and lock the current active orchestrator;
2. preserve its persisted mode unless the caller explicitly requests a different mode before creation;
3. create the replacement session with a fresh controller generation;
4. update the project conversation's current orchestrator binding;
5. record the exact old/new AO session IDs;
6. resume the same provider conversation when the driver can prove safe continuity;
7. otherwise start a new provider conversation and append a visible system boundary explaining that provider-native context restarted;
8. never reinterpret AO's durable history as provider model context unless the provider protocol explicitly supports that operation.

Changing the global default alone must not change the mode of a replacement orchestrator.

### Durable global preference

AO currently lacks a general daemon-owned user-preferences model. Introduce the smallest typed solution that can safely serve desktop, mobile, and CLI.

Preferred properties:

- a typed singleton settings record/table or equivalent daemon-owned store;
- `default_session_mode` constrained to `chat|tui`;
- default `tui` when absent;
- GET/PATCH service and controller boundary;
- atomic writes;
- API validation and stable error envelope;
- no Electron default app-data paths;
- no renderer-only source of truth.

Avoid adding unrelated settings in the same change.

## Chat conversation domain

Add a provider-neutral domain that is separate from terminal runtime ports.

Illustrative contract:

```go
type ConversationConnector interface {
    Probe(ctx context.Context, cfg ChatStartConfig) (ChatCapabilities, error)
    Start(ctx context.Context, cfg ChatStartConfig) (ConversationConnection, ConversationRef, error)
    Resume(ctx context.Context, cfg ChatResumeConfig) (ConversationConnection, error)
}

type ConversationConnection interface {
    Snapshot(ctx context.Context) (ProviderConversationSnapshot, error)
    Watch(ctx context.Context, cursor string, sink ProviderEventSink) error
    SendTurn(ctx context.Context, msg UserMessage) (TurnRef, error)
    Steer(ctx context.Context, turn TurnRef, msg UserMessage) error
    Interrupt(ctx context.Context, turn TurnRef) error
    ResolvePermission(ctx context.Context, requestID string, decision Decision) error
    Close() error
}
```

Exact method grouping is open to implementation, but the port must not:

- expose provider DTOs outside its adapter;
- depend on frontend types;
- use terminal byte streams as semantic events;
- treat an empty user message as Enter;
- mix shell-terminal lifecycle with provider conversation lifecycle.

### Capabilities

The agent catalog should expose structured capabilities independently of installation/auth status:

```text
chat
history
resume
streaming
tools
permissions
diffs
plans
interrupt
steer
queue
usage
models
```

Each capability should have an explicit status where necessary:

- supported;
- unsupported;
- experimental;
- temporarily unavailable due to version/auth/preflight.

Define a minimum production Chat capability set before enabling the Chat setting for a harness. At minimum, an agent that can mutate the workspace should not be considered Chat-ready unless permissions, errors, completion, and resume/recovery are safely represented.

## Provider-neutral projection and live protocol

Provider adapters normalize native events into AO turns/items and a small semantic live protocol. Persist durable item state; do not persist every token as a standalone domain event.

Suggested live envelope:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "liveEventSequence": 291,
  "streamGeneration": "daemon-generation-id",
  "conversationId": "conv-project-ao",
  "sessionId": "ao-12",
  "provider": "codex",
  "providerConversationId": "thr_...",
  "controllerGeneration": "gen_...",
  "type": "item.upsert",
  "payload": {
    "itemId": "item_...",
    "sequence": 42,
    "revision": 7
  }
}
```

Initial semantic stream types:

```text
subscribed
turn.upsert
item.upsert
action.upsert
message.delta
capabilities
controller.state
resync_required
error
```

Durable item kinds and typed `detail_json` represent tools, commands, diffs, plans, permissions, usage, delegations, summaries, and errors without leaking provider DTOs into the renderer.

Rules:

- preserve provider-native IDs as opaque correlation metadata;
- AO live event IDs/sequences and durable item sequences are provider-neutral;
- **durable item sequence and live stream sequence are different counters**;
- provider-specific additions do not leak into shared rendering components;
- streaming deltas update one item revision in place instead of allocating new timeline positions;
- final turn/item state and provider cursor flush immediately;
- intermediate deltas may be coalesced in memory and persisted at bounded intervals;
- terminal ANSI/control sequences never enter this protocol;
- large raw output is bounded and references durable artifacts when necessary;
- secrets and raw credentials are redacted before persistence or UI delivery;
- private/raw reasoning is excluded from the normalized model.

### Snapshot/subscription boundary

The snapshot must expose both counters:

```json
{
  "conversationId": "conv-project-ao",
  "scope": { "kind": "project", "projectId": "agent-orchestrator" },
  "currentOrchestratorSessionId": "ao-12",
  "latestItemSequence": 149,
  "liveEventCursor": 291,
  "streamGeneration": "daemon-generation-id",
  "capabilities": {},
  "controller": { "state": "connected", "error": null },
  "turns": [],
  "items": [],
  "hasMoreBefore": false
}
```

Client bootstrap:

1. fetch the authoritative durable snapshot;
2. render the returned turns/items;
3. subscribe to the semantic mux channel **after `liveEventCursor`**, never after `latestItemSequence`;
4. apply revision-aware deltas/upserts;
5. refetch/resubscribe when stream generation changes or a revision/cursor gap is detected.

This closes the snapshot/subscribe race without misusing SQLite CDC as a token stream.

### CDC versus semantic mux

- DB triggers emit compact invalidation events for durable conversation/turn/item/action/provider-state changes.
- Existing `/api/v1/events` CDC continues to invalidate/refetch session, PR, review, check, workspace, and conversation facts.
- Existing `/mux` gains a conversation channel for high-frequency semantic deltas and authoritative upserts.
- CDC payloads never become chat prose.
- Terminal payload buffering remains separate from semantic conversation backpressure.

Suggested mux subscription:

```json
{
  "ch": "conversation",
  "type": "subscribe",
  "conversationId": "conv-project-ao",
  "streamGeneration": "known-generation",
  "afterEventSequence": 291
}
```

Backpressure rules:

- coalesce message deltas approximately every 16–50 ms;
- keep at most one replaceable pending delta per streaming item;
- never drop a final upsert, completion, approval, action transition, or error;
- include base/current item revision where needed;
- revision gaps require a snapshot resync;
- bound semantic queues independently per client;
- disconnect a slow client rather than blocking provider readers.

## Message ordering, idempotency, and delivery

Use a per-session serialized command path:

```text
client input
  -> validate session/mode/capability
  -> assign clientMessageId/messageId
  -> persist queued intent
  -> controller queue/lease
  -> provider send
  -> persist accepted/rejected outcome
  -> stream provider events
```

Requirements:

- all AO send surfaces accept or generate a stable client message ID;
- duplicate client retries do not create duplicate provider turns;
- only one dispatch operation mutates a provider conversation at a time;
- mid-turn messages follow declared driver semantics:
  - steer when supported and explicitly intended;
  - otherwise queue until idle;
  - never paste into a permission dialog;
- uncertain provider acknowledgement is surfaced as uncertain rather than automatically retried;
- controller restart reconciliation resolves queued/in-flight records conservatively;
- automated messages use the same queue and do not bypass user messages;
- provider-generated sequence gaps trigger replay/reconciliation where supported.

The provider conversation is authoritative for model context. AO's durable event ledger is authoritative for product ordering, rendering, delivery state, and orchestration. AO must not maintain a second independently writable model transcript.

## Chat controller ownership and recovery

Each Chat session needs a single daemon-owned controller actor/worker:

- one live owner per `session_id`;
- one provider conversation ID;
- one controller generation;
- serialized commands;
- cancellation and shutdown;
- bounded reconnect/backoff;
- stale-generation event rejection;
- explicit health/readiness state.

On daemon restart:

1. read the persisted session mode;
2. do not start a native TUI for a Chat session;
3. resume the stored provider conversation;
4. reconcile provider history/status where supported;
5. project any missing durable events idempotently;
6. mark an interrupted/unknown turn honestly;
7. resume queued work only when duplicate execution is ruled out.

Do not silently create a new provider conversation when resume fails. Surface a recovery state with user choices such as retry, inspect diagnostics, or create a new session.

### Process supervision

V1 launches a daemon-managed Codex app-server and communicates through the app-server's default JSONL stdio transport.

Why stdio:

- it is the stable/default transport;
- the Go daemon is the only interactive provider client in Chat mode;
- no remote native TUI must attach;
- no new Unix socket, WebSocket, TCP listener, capability token, or Windows loopback transport is required;
- it removes multi-client approval ownership and remote backpressure from the V1 architecture.

The V1 spike must decide whether one daemon-managed app-server multiplexes several AO/Codex threads or each Chat session gets an isolated app-server process. Compare resource use, failure blast radius, configuration consistency, approval routing, and restart behavior before locking this process topology. Either topology still has one writable AO controller per provider thread.

Claude Agent SDK is a later provider. Its integration requires a packaging decision because AO's daemon is Go while the Agent SDK is exposed through supported non-Go runtimes. The likely shape is a small daemon-owned provider bridge/sidecar with structured local IPC. Requirements:

- it is backend infrastructure, not Electron renderer logic;
- ship it through the canonical desktop distribution;
- keep all runtime state under `~/.ao`;
- version/protocol handshake before session creation;
- no network listener beyond existing allowed AO boundaries;
- prefer stdio or a protected local IPC endpoint;
- log safely and redact secrets;
- expose health and graceful shutdown;
- support deterministic integration tests with a fake bridge.

Evaluate provider-by-provider whether a reconnectable broker is needed to preserve in-progress turns across daemon restarts. Provider session resume may recover completed context but not an actively executing turn.

## Provider adapters

### Codex app-server

Implement the first production Chat driver around the Codex app-server lifecycle:

- spawn and supervise app-server over stdio;
- initialize handshake;
- `thread/start`;
- persist returned thread ID;
- `turn/start` for user messages;
- streamed item/turn notifications;
- approvals;
- interrupt;

## Spawn architecture

Do not grow `session_manager.Manager.Spawn` into a large provider/mode conditional.

Refactor only as needed to establish real shared phases:

```text
resolve project/harness/mode/config
validate selected controller capability
create seed session with immutable mode
materialize/provision workspace
write attachments/system instructions
start exactly one controller:
  tui  -> existing Agent + Runtime path
  chat -> ChatDriver path
persist controller identity
mark lifecycle spawned
deliver initial prompt through the selected controller
```

Rollback must understand which resources exist:

- workspace created but no controller;
- TUI runtime created;
- Chat provider conversation created;
- shell terminal created independently;
- provider conversation created but AO persistence failed.

Chat rollback should not archive/delete provider history unless that destructive behavior is explicitly designed and tested. Prefer preserving recoverable provider context and recording an orphan/recovery fact.

## Restore, kill, cleanup, and reaper behavior

Every lifecycle operation must branch from persisted mode:

### Restore

- TUI: retain current native restore command/runtime behavior.
- Chat: resume the provider conversation through the Chat driver.
- never fall back across modes;
- rotate controller generation before accepting new events;
- preserve cleanup-generation fencing.

### Kill/terminate

- TUI: current runtime teardown.
- Chat: interrupt active turn, close driver/broker ownership, retain durable history according to provider policy, terminate session;
- shell terminals follow their existing cleanup semantics;
- a failed provider probe is not proof the session is dead.

### Reaper

- separate Chat controller liveness from shell terminal liveness;
- do not derive Chat death from a missing terminal handle;
- do not derive TUI death from a missing Chat driver;
- keep unknown probe results non-terminal;
- reconcile orphaned controller processes safely.

### Cleanup

- preserve current dirty-worktree safety;
- delete/archive chat event rows only under the session's explicit cleanup policy;
- avoid destructive provider-history deletion by default.

## Activity and status projection

Current activity derives from hooks and terminal/runtime observations. Add a mode-aware projector:

- Chat mode:
  - `turn.started` -> active;
  - permission/user-input request -> blocked/waiting input as appropriate;
  - completed turn -> waiting input/idle;
  - controller failure -> exited or a new durable fact feeding derived status;
- TUI mode:
  - preserve existing hook/activity behavior.

Rules:

- do not persist a second display status;
- continue deriving user-facing status from durable facts;
- disable or fence duplicate hook signals for Chat-mode provider processes;
- preserve SCM-derived status precedence;
- ensure a Chat permission resolution clears only the matching request;
- handle parallel/subagent tool events using stable IDs rather than tool-name heuristics.

## Security and trust boundaries

- Keep the primary daemon listener loopback-only and unauthenticated as designed.
- The opt-in LAN listener continues to require bearer-password middleware and must not gain control-only routes.
- Chat history/events exposed through mobile must follow existing LAN route/auth policy.
- Do not create a new network-facing provider bridge.
- Provider bridge local IPC must not be reachable by arbitrary network clients.
- Treat provider event payloads and command output as untrusted display data.
- Sanitize markdown/links and never render provider HTML directly.
- Redact secrets, tokens, environment values, and sensitive paths from durable logs/events where required.
- Permission decisions must be explicit typed actions; never derive them from a generic Send/Enter.
- Shell terminal remains a powerful local escape hatch and should preserve existing user expectations.
- All Electron state remains under `~/.ao/electron`; daemon/provider state remains under `~/.ao`.

## Failure modes and product handling

| Failure | Required behavior |
|---|---|
| Chat selected for unsupported harness | Reject with typed error; offer explicit TUI creation |
| Driver binary/bridge missing | Fail before durable creation when possible |
| Auth missing | Report auth-required and offer setup/retry; do not silently open native TUI |
| Provider protocol version mismatch | Mark driver incompatible and keep TUI available for new explicit sessions |
| Provider process exits before first prompt | Roll back safely or park recoverable terminated session with clear reason |
| Provider accepts turn but AO loses connection | Mark delivery uncertain; reconcile history before retry |
| Duplicate client retry | Return existing message/turn outcome |
| Daemon restarts during idle | Resume same provider conversation |
| Daemon restarts during active turn | Reattach/reconcile if supported; otherwise surface interrupted/unknown without duplicate execution |
| Permission request arrives while user sends | Serialize actions; never interpret send as permission resolution |
| Old controller emits after restore | Reject by generation |
| Shell survives while Chat driver dies | Keep shell available; show Chat recovery state |
| Chat driver survives while shell exits | Chat continues; allow opening a new shell |
| User manually starts native agent in shell | It is unmanaged and not merged into AO Chat |
| Setting changes with live sessions | Live sessions unchanged |
| History is very large | Page/virtualize; do not load entire transcript synchronously |
| Unknown provider event | Retain bounded diagnostics; do not guess semantic UI |

## Open decisions

The product architecture is settled by this issue. These bounded implementation decisions remain for Phase 0/spikes:

1. Does V1 use one daemon-managed Codex app-server with multiple threads or one process per Chat session?
2. What exact tested capability/version floor makes an installed Codex build Chat-ready?
3. What are the size/retention limits for command output, diffs, item detail, and conversation history?
4. Can an active Codex turn be reattached after daemon failure, or must some crash boundaries settle as interrupted/uncertain?
5. Can `/send` evolve compatibly for Chat acknowledgement, or should it delegate to a new canonical `/messages` response contract?
6. How long is AO Chat history retained after session cleanup, and is provider-owned history ever archived/deleted?
7. Is documentation sufficient for manually launching a provider CLI in a Chat shell, or should AO show a contextual warning?
8. What performance threshold triggers timeline virtualization beyond paginated history?
9. When, if ever, should Chat become the default for new installations? This is a later rollout decision, not part of V1.

The following are **not** open:

- Codex app-server is the first production Chat provider.
- V1 uses app-server stdio, not remote native TUI attachment.
- Chat/TUI is immutable per session.
- Chat-mode Terminal is a plain worktree shell.
- structured approvals are required for mutating Chat V1.
- orchestrator conversation is project-scoped and worker conversation is session-scoped.
- existing sessions remain TUI and are not reconstructed from terminal output.
- Claude Agent SDK follows the Codex vertical slice.

## Alternatives considered

### Chat UI plus writable native TUI for the same session

Rejected. Two independent provider clients can race and diverge even when initialized with the same conversation ID.

### Move a conversation back and forth between SDK and TUI

Not part of the initial design. Serialized ownership handoff is provider-specific, difficult to make crash-safe, and unnecessary when each session has a fixed mode.

### Treat Chat/TUI as a frontend tab preference

Rejected. CLI, mobile, internal reactions, restore, and reaper behavior would still use ambiguous controller paths.

### Use terminal output as the Chat transcript

Rejected. PTY bytes are ephemeral presentation data without stable message/tool/permission identity.

### Remove terminals entirely

Rejected. Chat mode retains a normal session-scoped worktree shell; TUI mode remains available for compatibility and provider-native workflows.

### Silently fall back from Chat to TUI

Rejected. It violates user intent and obscures provider capability gaps. Fallback must be explicit before session creation.

## Before submitting

- [x] Searched open issues for similar Chat UI / TUI / session-mode work.
- [x] Grounded the plan in the current Go daemon, SQLite/CDC, API generation, Electron renderer, terminal mux, session-scoped shell, CLI, and lifecycle boundaries.

title: fix: retain terminal viewport across navigation
body:
## Summary

- retain each lazily visited terminal renderer for its authoritative logical session plus terminal handle/generation lifetime
- reject stale routed shell/reviewer targets synchronously and replace reviewer renderers when a new run reuses a handle
- park inactive terminals hidden, inert, blurred, and unable to send input or resize while continuing to parse live output
- restore canonical bottom-follow or a marker-backed historical viewport before revealing the retained terminal
- share one browser-to-daemon mux WebSocket across independently owned terminal attachment leases
- preserve exited/error scrollback and Restore controls, badge URLs from hidden sessions, and clean up on authoritative lifecycle boundaries
- add deterministic real-xterm Chromium coverage for six live sessions, frame-sensitive reveal, reconnect, cleanup, scrollback eviction, and handle replacement

## Root cause

After #3185, navigating away still unmounted TerminalPane, xterm, and its attachment. Returning created a fresh attachment, so tmux replayed terminal state into a new buffer. Replay buffering reduced the visible walk but could not preserve the user-scrolled historical viewport, selection, or renderer state. A retained terminal could also expose a stale offscreen DOM scrollbar for one frame unless its canonical xterm buffer position and DOM viewport were synchronized before reveal.

The fix moves renderer and attachment ownership above routed session views. It does not add another timeout or extend the replay cover.

Follow-up to #3185 and #3160.

## User impact

Returning to a previously visited terminal restores the same xterm instance, selection, content anchor, and viewport. Hidden output advances the buffer without forcing a scrolled-up viewport to the bottom; terminals left at the bottom continue following output. Rapid A-B-A switching does not create duplicate writers or expose an intermediate replay frame.

Exact historical-anchor restoration is bounded by xterm's existing 5,000-line scrollback. This patch does not reduce terminal history. If enough hidden output evicts the selected line, return clamps once to the oldest retained line instead of replay-scrolling or jumping repeatedly.

The behavior is provider-independent: Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode/Kilo, reviewer terminals, and standalone shells all use the same terminal ownership layer.

## Validation

- focused Vitest: 5 files, 185 tests passed
- full renderer Vitest: 95 files, 1,291 tests passed
- frontend typecheck and E2E typecheck: passed
- isolated Chromium terminal/smoke run: 6 tests passed
- real-xterm cases cover six retained sessions, hidden/return-time output, bottom and historical anchors, reconnect, resize/fit, rapid A-B-A, empty/short replay, selection, scrollback eviction, generation replacement, one socket/multiple writers, and cleanup
- production macOS arm64 package: passed
- git diff check: passed

## Residual risk

A genuine terminal grid change still relies on the existing resize/SIGWINCH protocol, which has no explicit acknowledgement that a full-screen terminal application completed its repaint. The retained xterm is fitted and synchronized before reveal, but a runtime-specific repaint can arrive afterward. This was not observed in the supplied recordings, Chromium integration tests, or manual validation.

title: fix(inspector): dedup PR summaries across whole merged result
body:
Fixes #3242

## Problem

The Session Inspector Summary tab accumulates pull requests from other sessions and duplicates entries when cycling between sessions. The header count (`PULL REQUESTS (2)`) disagrees with the rendered list (7+ cards).

Root cause: `sessionPRDisplaySummaries` deduped summaries against session PR facts, but not **within** the summaries array itself. If the `GET /sessions/{id}/pr` API returned duplicate entries (or CDC events caused PR accumulation), every copy rendered — and the list grew monotonically with each session switch.

## Fix

Replace the `facts → seen-set → append-remaining-summaries` pattern with a `Map<number, SessionPRSummary>` keyed by PR number. This guarantees each PR appears at most once regardless of how many times it appears across either source, and the insertion order (facts first, extra summaries second) is preserved before final sort.

## Test coverage

- **Duplicate summaries**: two entries with the same PR number → one result
- **Cross-session isolation**: two sessions with different PRs → each returns only its own
- **Facts + summaries merge**: enriched summary replaces fact for the same PR number
- **Summary-only PR**: a PR present only in summaries (no fact) is included
- **No PRs**: empty session returns empty list
- All 96 test files / 1286 tests pass, typecheck clean

title: Reuse /review command for review terminals for the agent harness that support it
body:
## Summary This issue is an analysis of whether AO should use harness-native review commands for reviewer terminals. The current focus is Codex's `/review` command. Claude Code support is coming soon. The purpose of this issue is to compare the possible architectures and decide whether the functionality provided by Codex `/review` justifies changing AO's existing reviewer architecture. ## Approaches considered | Approach | Pros | Cons | |---|---|---| | **1. Existing AO approach**
Dedicated reviewer agent with AO's own prompt | Clean separation from the worker; durable review runs; supports retries, cancellation, status, and multiple harnesses; good Diff/Reviews UI integration; full AO control | AO must maintain its own review rubric and output parsing; it does not automatically use Codex's built-in `/review` behavior | | **2. New session running `/review`** | Uses Codex's built-in review rubric; standard findings and priorities; isolated from the worker; simple review experience | Extra session, cost, and latency; AO still needs result parsing and persistence; must handle stale commits; custom AO instructions may conflict with Codex's rubric | | **3. `/review` as a worker sub-agent** | Reuses worker context; potentially faster; natural parent-child relationship; can appear under the worker | Creates nested review semantics; inherits worker bias and context; harder permission isolation; no automatic Diff-tab integration; adds complexity without a clear quality benefit | | **4. `/review` inside the reviewer harness** | Preserves AO's reviewer-run architecture; Codex can use its native review behavior; keeps the reviewer separate from the worker; works as one harness among many | AO and Codex prompts may overlap or conflict; behavior can change with Codex versions; AO still owns lifecycle, parsing, persistence, and UI integration; the harness must avoid creating another nested review layer | ## What Codex `/review` provides Codex `/review` provides a useful review rubric, target selection, prioritized findings, and conventional PR-review behavior. It does not provide AO's durable review-run lifecycle, stale-commit handling, reviewer isolation, persistence, worker feedback delivery, or Diff-tab integration. AO would still need to build and maintain those pieces around it. ## Architectural comparison The options below are alternatives being evaluated, not implementation requirements. ```text AO review run -> Codex reviewer harness -> one Codex review invocation -> exact target SHA -> structured findings -> AO persists and renders the result ``` ## Decision Do not change AO's reviewer architecture to use Codex `/review`. The command's benefits are mostly prompt and workflow conveniences. They do not materially improve the capabilities AO needs from a reviewer: durable lifecycle management, exact review-target tracking, isolation, structured persistence, UI integration, and delivery of feedback to the worker. Introducing `/review` would add session complexity, nested review semantics, additional token usage and latency, prompt precedence concerns, version coupling to Codex internals, and more edge cases around stale worktrees and output parsing. A worker sub-agent that invokes `/review` would additionally inherit worker context and bias while making permission isolation harder. The existing AO reviewer flow already provides the important product capabilities. AO can reproduce the useful parts of the Codex review rubric in its reviewer prompt without adopting the native command or creating another session layer. ### Final recommendation Keep the current architecture and do not implement Codex `/review` integration as part of this issue. Revisit only if Codex exposes additional functionality that AO cannot reasonably reproduce through its existing reviewer prompt and lifecycle. Claude Code native review support is coming soon and should be evaluated separately using the same standard: native-command functionality must provide substantial value beyond AO's existing reviewer flow before it justifies architectural changes.

title: `ao session ls` hides orchestrator-kind sessions → operators spawn duplicate orchestrators unknowingly
body:
## Summary
The session listing (`ao session ls`) omits sessions of kind `orchestrator`. Because the default listing is the primary way an operator checks "what's already running," an orchestrator that already exists is invisible there — so the operator (or an automation) spawns a second orchestrator for the same project. Multiple orchestrators then run against the same worktree/board, competing: duplicate dispatches, conflicting merges, and one orchestrator reaping the other's workers.

## Impact
- Silent duplicate orchestrators per project; wasted spend and contradictory actions.
- Hard to diagnose: the very command used to check state is the one that hides the cause.
- A dead/duplicate orchestrator surfaces later as a confusing "No conversation found with session ID …" when someone clicks through to it.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Start an orchestrator for a project.
2. Run `ao session ls` — the orchestrator is not listed.
3. Lacking any signal that one exists, start another orchestrator for the same project.
4. Observe two orchestrators dispatching/merging against the same target.

## Root cause
The listing filters out the `orchestrator` session kind (only `ao orchestrator ls` shows them). The two surfaces are separate, so the common path gives a false "nothing is running."

## Proposed fix (any one, ideally 1+3)
1. **Include orchestrators in `ao session ls`** with a clear `KIND` column (or a visible `— orchestrators hidden, see \`ao orchestrator ls\`` footer when any exist).
2. **Guard against duplicates at spawn:** when creating an orchestrator for a project that already has a live one, refuse (or require `--force`) with a pointer to the existing one.
3. **Reconcile on spawn:** detect an existing live orchestrator for the same project/worktree and attach/adopt rather than create a second.

## Acceptance
- With a live orchestrator, the default listing makes its existence discoverable (fix 1), **and/or**
- spawning a second orchestrator for the same project is blocked or explicitly warned (fix 2/3),
- covered by a test asserting a second same-project orchestrator spawn is prevented or surfaced.

## Design and official Cursor constraints

The adapter follows the OpenCode reviewer shape: a dedicated reviewer wrapper supplies command, message, and cancellation behavior; the central launcher owns workspace/runtime execution and executable preflight; AO-owned system/task files contain the review instructions; and results are recorded through the existing `ao review submit` boundary rather than parsed from terminal output.

Official references reviewed:

- CLI overview/executable: https://docs.cursor.com/en/cli/overview
- headless print mode: https://docs.cursor.com/en/cli/headless
- parameters: https://docs.cursor.com/en/cli/reference/parameters
- authentication (`cursor-agent login/status`, `CURSOR_API_KEY`): https://docs.cursor.com/en/cli/reference/authentication
- output and nonzero failure semantics: https://docs.cursor.com/en/cli/reference/output-format
- config-file permissions: https://docs.cursor.com/cli/reference/permissions
- Ask mode: https://cursor.com/changelog/cli-jan-16-2026
- official repositories: https://github.com/cursor

Cursor exposes permissions through configuration files rather than a per-invocation tool allowlist. This integration uses Ask mode for non-editing review analysis and `--force` so the required git inspection and `gh`/`ao review submit` reporting commands do not wait for interactive approval.

## Integration surfaces

- new `backend/internal/adapters/reviewer/cursor` adapter and focused tests
- reviewer domain vocabulary and registry
- project config validation and worker-harness fallback resolution
- desktop project-settings reviewer selection and test coverage
- README reviewer list

No HTTP DTO changed, so OpenAPI/frontend schema regeneration was not required.

## Verification

- `go test ./internal/adapters/reviewer/... ./internal/domain ./internal/review` — passed
- `go test ./internal/adapters/agent/kilocode -run TestAuthStatusUnknownWhenKeyOnlyComesFromInteractiveShell -count=1` — passed on isolated rerun

- AO does not parse Cursor text output; the reviewer must complete the existing GitHub review plus `ao review submit` workflow.

body:
## Summary

End-to-end UI overhaul on the `feat/ui-revamp` branch. Changes are cumulative across many sessions; this PR lands them all.

### Design system
- New token layer in `tokens.css`: border radii, spacing scale, window/panel geometry, easing curves, and animation keyframes as CSS custom properties
- Removed `font-mono` from all UI chrome; Geist Sans throughout, Geist Mono only in terminals
- Global `scrollbar-width: none` — no scrollbars anywhere in the app
- Active/hover surfaces use `bg-interactive-active` / `bg-interactive-hover`; removed bespoke one-off colours

### Sidebar
- Animated open/close with Framer Motion spring (no animation on first mount / app reload)
- Floating sidebar peek: hovering within 60px of the left edge shows a real offset peek of the sidebar; within 25px shows it fully
- Projects collapsed by default; folder icon click toggles, row click navigates (or expands if collapsed)
- Project avatar: two-letter monogram with a generated oklch colour pair, persisted per project

title: feat(review): add interactive reviewers for all agent harnesses
body:
## Summary

Adds interactive code-review support for every currently supported AO agent harness. Reviewers run in persistent terminal sessions, receive an AO-owned review prompt, inspect the target change, and submit structured findings through the existing review flow.

This PR expands the reviewer catalog from Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode to **23 reviewer adapters**:

- Agy, Aider, Amp, Auggie, Autohand, Cline, Continue, Copilot, Crush, Cursor
- Devin, Droid, Goose, Grok, Kilo Code, Kimi, Kiro, Pi, Qwen, and Vibe
- Existing Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode reviewers remain supported

It also exposes the complete catalog in project settings and adds documentation and test coverage for reviewer selection and launch behavior.

## How reviewers work

- Reviewers launch as interactive TUIs in persistent runtime panes.
- AO injects a reviewer-specific system/task prompt that requires read-only analysis and structured review submission.
- Later review tasks reuse a healthy pane; stopped or superseded panes are replaced safely.
- Cancellation uses the adapter's supported interrupt behavior, including native Escape handling where required.
- Reviewer configuration is separate from worker and orchestrator configuration; a project must select the reviewer it wants.

## Reviewer behavior matrix

| Reviewer | Session behavior | How AO constrains the reviewer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | Persistent interactive pane | AO reviewer system prompt through the native Claude adapter; automatic permission mode, so prompt policy is part of the trust boundary |
| Codex | Persistent interactive pane | AO reviewer system prompt through the native Codex adapter, with Codex's native approval/sandbox configuration |
| OpenCode | Persistent interactive pane | AO reviewer system prompt through the native OpenCode adapter; automatic permission mode, so prompt policy is part of the trust boundary |
| Cursor | Persistent interactive pane | Private AO-owned reviewer profile and restrictive allow/deny configuration; no force, YOLO, or headless flags |
| Kilo Code | Persistent interactive pane | Hidden reviewer-agent configuration, isolated project resources, and an explicit read/report-only policy |
| Copilot | Persistent interactive pane | AO-owned profile with granular tool allow/deny rules; broad allow-all flags are not enabled |
| Pi | Persistent interactive pane | Resource discovery and built-in tools disabled; an AO-owned extension exposes bounded reads, fixed Git inspection, and structured submission only |
| Kiro | Persistent interactive pane | Runs from an AO-owned neutral directory with a private reviewer agent and deny-by-default shell policy |
| Amp | Persistent interactive pane | AO-owned settings plus the reviewer system prompt; readiness markers are used before task delivery |
| Aider | **Fresh process per review pass** | AO supplies the system and task prompt files as read-only context; the process is request-scoped |
| Agy | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental host-trusted** mode; restrictive prompt/CLI setup reduces accidental edits but is not OS isolation |
| Continue | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental host-trusted** mode; launches in an AO-owned neutral directory and receives the task after readiness |
| Devin | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental host-trusted** mode; AO injects the reviewer role, but the provider does not expose enforceable cross-platform containment |
| Droid | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental host-trusted** mode; AO injects the reviewer role, but the provider does not expose enforceable cross-platform containment |
| Goose | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental host-trusted** mode with a constrained reviewer configuration; not an OS sandbox |
| Kimi | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental host-trusted** mode; restrictive launch shape and prompt policy, without OS-level isolation |
| Qwen | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental host-trusted** mode from an AO-owned neutral directory; task is delivered after readiness and Escape cancels the active turn |
| Vibe | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental host-trusted** plan mode; restrictive mode reduces accidental authority but is not OS isolation |
| Grok | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental user-approved** mode; AO supplies the reviewer role and keeps native permission prompts enabled |
| Crush | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental user-approved** mode; AO supplies the reviewer role and keeps native permission prompts enabled |
| Auggie | **Fresh process per review pass** | **Experimental user-approved** mode using native rules/permission prompts; the process lifecycle is request-scoped |
| Cline | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental user-approved** mode; system instructions are injected without enabling auto-approval |
| Autohand | Persistent interactive pane | **Experimental user-approved** mode; AO supplies the system prompt and leaves native approvals enabled |

All 23 adapters use an interactive terminal UI. “Host-trusted” means the no-edit rule is enforced primarily by prompt and restrictive provider modes, not by an AO-controlled OS sandbox. These reviewers must therefore be selected explicitly.

## Safety model

- Hardened adapters use provider-specific controls such as isolated AO-owned configuration, restricted tools, permission flags, or the secure reviewer gateway.
- Adapters without enforceable CLI containment are clearly treated as **host-trusted/experimental** and require explicit selection. Their prompts prohibit file edits, but prompts are guidance rather than an OS sandbox.
- Reviewer launch fails closed when required binaries, versions, capabilities, or runtime prerequisites are unavailable.
- The launcher verifies readiness before reusing a pane and avoids delivering tasks to stale or superseded sessions.

## Notable infrastructure

- Adds the provider-neutral secure TUI gateway and capability manifests.
- Adds constrained checkout/prompt reads, fixed read-only Git operations, and structured GitHub/AO review submission.
- Extends tmux and ConPTY runtime support for interactive reviewer cancellation and lifecycle handling.
- Adds reviewer availability and trust-state messaging to project settings.

## Verification

- All 11 GitHub CI checks pass on the current head.
- Backend reviewer, review launcher, gateway, domain, controller, and runtime tests pass.
- Frontend reviewer settings tests and TypeScript checks pass.
- Adapter tests cover command shape, prompt delivery, cancellation, readiness, pane reuse, and fail-closed behavior.

These are deterministic unit/integration checks using fake runtimes and command assertions. They do not claim live end-to-end authentication or review execution against every third-party provider.

## Supersedes

- #3380
- #3381
- #3382

title: [Feature]: Add adapter-aware worker and orchestrator model selection
body:
## Problem

AO lets users choose separate worker and orchestrator agents, but it does not provide a reliable, role-specific way to select the model used by each agent.

Users currently have to know and manually enter adapter-specific model identifiers. The available models differ by agent:

- Claude Code and Codex have their own supported model families and aliases.
- Some agent CLIs expose a non-interactive model-list command.
- Some adapters accept a model override but do not expose a discoverable catalog.
- Amp exposes execution modes (`low`, `medium`, `high`, and `ultra`) rather than model identifiers.

A single hard-coded global list will become stale and cannot accurately represent all adapters. Querying every CLI on every settings render would also be slow and unnecessarily expensive.

## Proposed direction

Add an adapter-aware model selector to Project Settings, with independent values for the worker and orchestrator roles.

AO should use three catalog strategies:

1. **Curated catalog** for agents with stable, documented model aliases or product-specific models.
2. **CLI discovery** when the installed agent exposes a documented, non-interactive model-list command.
3. **Free-text fallback** when AO cannot reliably discover a model list.

Amp should use a constrained mode selector instead of a model input.

### User experience

- Show a model field immediately below the selected worker agent.
- Show a separate model field immediately below the selected orchestrator agent.
- For a catalog, provide searchable suggestions while still allowing custom IDs when supported.
- For adapters without discovery, provide a free-text input.
- For Amp, provide a mode menu with `low`, `medium`, `high`, and `ultra`.
- Selecting the empty/default value should let the agent choose its own default.
- Changing an agent should clear the model/mode previously selected for that role.
- Provide a refresh action for each role's catalog.
- If refresh fails, retain the last successful cached catalog and show a warning.

## Adapter coverage

AO currently ships 23 production agent adapters. The intended initial strategy is:

### Curated catalog

- Claude Code
- Codex

### Mode selector

- Amp

### CLI-discovered catalog

- AGY
- Aider
- Auggie
- Autohand
- Cursor
- Devin
- Grok
- Kimi
- Kiro
- Kilo Code
- OpenCode
- Pi

### Free-text fallback

- Cline
- Continue
- Copilot
- Crush
- Droid
- Goose
- Qwen
- Vibe

Discovery commands should be kept in the backend and executed only with static adapter-defined arguments. A failed or unsupported command must never prevent project settings from being used.

## Backend and cache design

- Normalize all model sources into one daemon response:
  - agent ID
  - selection mode (`catalog`, `text`, or `mode`)
  - model ID and display label
  - optional provider and default metadata
  - whether custom values are allowed
  - source
  - fetch timestamp
  - stale state and warning
- Add daemon endpoints to read and explicitly refresh one agent catalog.
- Persist successful catalogs in SQLite, keyed by agent and project scope.
- Record the installed agent binary version with the cached catalog.
- Reuse a cache entry while the installed version matches.
- Automatically rediscover after an installed agent version changes.
- On discovery failure:
  - return the previous catalog as stale when available;
  - otherwise return a free-text/custom-value fallback.
- Apply a short timeout to all CLI discovery commands.
- Do not add network requests to unit tests.

Suggested endpoints:

```text
GET  /api/v1/agents/{agent}/models?projectId={projectId}
POST /api/v1/agents/{agent}/models/refresh?projectId={projectId}
```

## Configuration and compatibility

- Store model/mode overrides in `worker.agentConfig` and `orchestrator.agentConfig`.
- Continue reading the legacy project-level `agentConfig.model` as a fallback.
- When settings are saved, migrate the displayed legacy value into the applicable role configurations without dropping unrelated shared settings such as permissions.
- Ensure every production adapter declares support for either a model or mode configuration field.
- Ensure model/mode overrides are forwarded consistently during both launch and restore.

The following adapters need explicit model forwarding coverage where it is currently incomplete:

- Aider
- Continue
- Cursor
- Devin
- Droid
- Grok
- OpenCode

Amp needs execution-mode forwarding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Worker and orchestrator model values can be selected independently.
- [ ] Claude Code and Codex expose curated model suggestions.
- [ ] Amp exposes its supported modes instead of a model input.
- [ ] Adapters with documented discovery commands return normalized catalogs.
- [ ] Remaining adapters accept a free-text model ID.
- [ ] Custom model IDs remain possible where the catalog permits them.
- [ ] Successful catalogs persist across daemon restarts.
- [ ] Catalogs are reused until manually refreshed or the installed agent version changes.
- [ ] Discovery errors fall back safely and do not block settings.
- [ ] Selected model/mode values are forwarded during launch and restore.
- [ ] Existing project-level model configuration remains backward compatible.
- [ ] All 23 production adapters report model or mode configuration capability.
- [ ] OpenAPI and frontend client types are regenerated together.
- [ ] Backend tests cover discovery parsing, cache reuse, refresh, stale fallback, API behavior, configuration merging, and adapter argument forwarding.
- [ ] Frontend tests cover role-specific values, legacy migration, refresh behavior, and catalog/text/mode rendering.

## Alternatives considered

### Maintain one hard-coded list for every adapter

This would avoid executing CLIs, but it would require frequent AO releases merely to keep provider model names current. It also cannot represent models supplied by locally configured providers.

### Always call each agent's `/model` or model-list command

This keeps data current but creates unnecessary process startup load, makes settings slow, and may trigger interactive or authentication-dependent behavior.

### Only provide free-text inputs

This scales technically but gives users no discoverability and makes invalid model identifiers more likely.

### Fetch all adapters at application startup

This adds latency and process load for agents the user may never select. Lazy discovery per selected agent, backed by persistent caching and explicit refresh, provides a better default. A separate “refresh all installed agents” action can be added later if needed.

## Out of scope

- Installing missing agent CLIs.
- Verifying provider-account authorization for each returned model.
- Automatically replacing saved values when a provider deprecates a model.
- Refreshing every adapter at every AO startup.
- A background “refresh all catalogs” workflow.

## Before submitting

- [x] I searched existing issues and discussions for something similar.
- [x] I am willing to help implement this if maintainers agree on scope.

title: feat: add adapter-aware model selection
body:
## Summary

Adds adapter-aware model and mode selection for independent worker and orchestrator roles. AO loads catalogs only for agents selected in Project Settings, combines curated values, safe CLI discovery, and declarative local configuration, then stores the normalized result in a project-scoped cache.

Users get a searchable selector when models are known and a custom text field when they are not. Worker and orchestrator choices remain independent.

## User-facing behavior

- Worker and orchestrator each have their own model or mode control.
- Claude Code and Codex use curated model catalogs.
- Amp exposes low, medium, high, and ultra modes.
- Supported CLI-backed agents discover models lazily through documented non-interactive commands.
- Crush, Continue, OpenCode, Qwen, and Kimi also contribute configured/custom models from safe local config parsing.
- Catalogs are searchable by model label or ID and retain a Custom model escape hatch.
- Agents without a reliable catalog use free-text input.
- Refresh failures retain the last useful catalog and show a warning.

## Discovery and caching

AO does not invoke all 23 adapters when settings opens. The frontend requests catalogs only for the currently selected worker and orchestrator agents.

The daemon merges and deduplicates model metadata from these sources:

| Source | Agents/use |
|---|---|
| Curated catalog | Claude Code, Codex |
| Curated mode list | Amp |
| Isolated CLI discovery | Agents with documented non-interactive list commands |
| Declarative config | Crush, Continue, OpenCode, Qwen, Kimi |
| Manual fallback | Agents with no reliable discovery source |

Catalogs are cached in SQLite by agent and project. Cache invalidation accounts for the installed binary version and a non-sensitive config metadata fingerprint. Explicit refresh bypasses the cache.

If CLI discovery fails but configuration yields models, AO returns and caches the partial catalog with a warning. If discovery fails with a previous cache, the previous catalog is returned as stale. If no usable result or cache exists, AO returns the free-text fallback contract.

## Portable configuration discovery

Config candidates follow each agent's documented precedence and are derived from the runtime OS and environment instead of this contributor's machine. Candidate paths are deduplicated and included in cache invalidation.

| Agent | Supported config locations |
|---|---|
| Crush | `CRUSH_GLOBAL_CONFIG`, `CRUSH_GLOBAL_DATA`, XDG/default user config and data, Windows `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, bounded project `crush.json`/`.crush.json`, current `crush.json`, and legacy Catwalk `providers.json`/`CRUSH_DATA_DIR` |
| Continue | OS user home `~/.continue/config.yaml` (plus `.yml` compatibility) and the existing project-local `.continue` compatibility files; Continue does not publish a stable filesystem pointer for the last `/config` selection |
| OpenCode | XDG/default global config, `OPENCODE_CONFIG`, `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR`, bounded nested project `opencode.json(c)`, `.opencode/opencode.json(c)`, and Linux/macOS/Windows managed JSON directories |
| Qwen | `QWEN_HOME`, project `.qwen/settings.json`, system defaults/settings on Linux/macOS/Windows, and both `QWEN_CODE_SYSTEM_*_PATH` overrides |
| Kimi | `KIMI_CODE_HOME/config.toml` or the portable `~/.kimi-code/config.toml` default |

The parsers support current and legacy Crush layouts and current/legacy Qwen `modelProviders` layouts, producing model IDs in the format each adapter can launch.

## Configuration security

Configuration discovery reads only bounded adapter-owned paths and extracts model ID, label, provider, and default state.

- JSON, JSONC, YAML, and standard TOML parsing
- 4 MiB maximum file size
- regular files only; symbolic links and unsafe traversal are rejected
- no execution of plugins, commands, imports, substitutions, or file references
- no caching of API keys, tokens, headers, endpoints, credentials, or raw config
- OpenCode CLI discovery always runs with `--pure` so project plugins cannot execute

## Backend and API

- Adds project-scoped agent model catalog persistence using migration 0041.
- Adds `GET /api/v1/agents/{agent}/models`.
- Adds `POST /api/v1/agents/{agent}/models/refresh`.
- Preserves model and Amp mode through domain, API, project configuration, and the CLI hand-mirrored DTO.
- Completes model forwarding for affected launch and restore adapters.
- Keeps legacy project-level model values readable and migrates displayed values to `worker.agentConfig` and `orchestrator.agentConfig` on save without dropping shared permissions.

## Intentional omissions

- No startup refresh of every adapter.
- No provider-account authorization check for individual models.
- No installation of missing agent CLIs.
- No automatic replacement of deprecated saved models.
- No filesystem-wide search or guessed undocumented config paths.
- Continue's saved runtime config selection is not read because Continue does not expose a stable documented local pointer for it; the documented default remains supported.
- Aider, Autohand, and other adapters without safe complete discovery remain free-text.

## Verification

Completed locally:

- focused backend tests for all five config-backed adapters
- race tests for model catalog and agent service
- cross-compilation of model catalog tests for Windows and Linux from macOS
- `golangci-lint` v2.12.2: 0 issues
- full backend package run; unrelated timing-sensitive fake/Kilo/OpenCode/tmux tests failed only under concurrent suite load and passed when rerun independently
- prior API generation, frontend typecheck/tests, renderer smoke, storage migration, and CLI round-trip coverage from this PR

Coverage includes platform and environment path precedence, nested Git-worktree lookup, current/legacy Crush and Qwen parsing, JSONC comments/trailing commas, YAML, TOML escapes, credential exclusion, file-size limits, symlink rejection, source merging, partial fallback, cache invalidation, API/service behavior, searchable filtering, refresh warnings, CLI model/mode round trips, migration behavior, and launch/restore forwarding.
